method: The page holds the ANSI/TIA-568 pin-to-pair table for an eight-conductor 100-ohm lead terminated on 8P8C plugs. Each standard lists eight pins in order: T568A is white/green, green, white/orange, blue, white/blue, orange, white/brown, brown from pin 1 to pin 8, and T568B is white/orange, orange, white/green, blue, white/blue, green, white/brown, brown. Pair 1 is blue and sits on pins 4-5 in both standards, pair 4 is brown on pins 7-8 in both, and pair 2 (orange) and pair 3 (green) take pins 1-2 and 3-6 in the opposite order in the two standards, so the pair grouping pins 1-2, 3-6, 4-5 and 7-8 is the same everywhere and no pair ever straddles another pair's pins. The page joins pin n at the left plug to pin n at the right plug, the way a lead is actually wired, then reports every pin's colour, its pair number and pair name at both ends and regroups the pins by pair at each end. A pair is continuous when it reaches the same two pins at the far end; the lead is straight-through when all four pairs are continuous, and a crossover when pairs 2 and 3 are the only pairs that move, which is exactly what pairing a T568A plug with a T568B plug does. Any other pattern is reported as mixed wiring, with each pair listed against the pins it actually occupies. Both ends accept T568A or T568B in either case, and anything else - a blank end, an unknown code such as T568C, or a cable category such as Cat6 - is refused by name rather than defaulted. The page reports the eight plug pins only: it does not model shielded or screened plugs, the colour code printed on a keystone jack's rear block, the polarity a PoE injector applies, or cable performance such as category or length. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

sources.title: ANSI/TIA-568-E, Commercial Building Telecommunications Cabling Standard: the T568A and T568B pin-to-pair assignments for the 8P8C plug, where T568A puts pair 3 on pins 1-2 and pair 2 on pins 3-6, T568B the reverse, and both keep pair 1 on pins 4-5 and pair 4 on 7-8
IEEE 802.3 Ethernet: 10BASE-T and 100BASE-TX use only pins 1-2 (transmit) and 3-6 (receive), while 1000BASE-T and faster use all four pairs
IEEE 802.3af/at Power over Ethernet: Alternative A delivers power on the data pairs (pins 1-2 and 3-6) and Alternative B on the spare pairs (pins 4-5 and 7-8)
